catalog_quote: [p.173] Stress is phonemic in Kanakanabu, and in all dialects of Rukai except Mantauran ... In Thao stress has a very small functional load (about 98% of all base morphemes are stressed on the penult, and the remaining 2% on the final syllable). In this language it is clearly of secondary origin. ... [p.407] In Thao of central Taiwan, for example, where stress is penultimate in about 98% of all forms (and final in the rest) ... [p.412] All three of these languages have penultimate stress, with minor qualifications (about 2% of Thao forms are oxytone, and in Amis stress is final in citation forms, but penultimate in phrasal context). ... [p.659] In addition to tonogenesis some AN languages have developed a historically secondary phonemic stress. The case of Mayá has already been noted. Other cases include Thao of central Taiwan, Rukai of south-central Taiwan, Pangasinan of central Luzon,…

new_statements.quote: [p.21] 邵語的單音節詞是當然的唯一重音，如shnaw（心），而有些語法結構上的限定詞如：ti, tu, sa, wa, ya則是平調無重音的。二個音節以上的詞，重音規則為落在詞的倒數第二音節，例如mú.shnaw（愛，喜歡）、bú.hat（田園）。加前綴或重疊音節時重音不受影響，如mu.bú.hat（工作），mu.buha.bú.hat（不斷工作），但是加後綴時則重音必須隨著後移，如shi.bu.há.tan（做過工作的地方）。[p.22] 邵語的「外來語」重音常在末尾音節以長音的方式表現，如/ʃinʃí:/先生醫生，/saukhá:/廚房灶腳，/saipú:/菜脯，/baksá:ŋ/粽子……邵語的重音位置基本上為倒數第二音節，但是如果後綴是-uan、-iza，則仍保留原詞幹的重音位置，但該詞幹尾音節的韻尾輔音延長成為-uan或-iza的開頭聲母，再於倒數第二音節唸重音。如果是-uan-iza的複合後綴，則重音甚至於可達三處之多。
new_statements.translation: [p.21] Monosyllabic words in Thao naturally carry the only stress, e.g. shnaw 'heart', while certain grammatical determiners such as ti, tu, sa, wa, ya are level-toned and unstressed. For words of two or more syllables the stress rule is that stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, e.g. mú.shnaw 'love, like', bú.hat 'field'. Adding a prefix or reduplicating a syllable does not affect the stress, e.g. mu.bú.hat 'work', mu.buha.bú.hat 'work continuously', but when a suffix is added the stress must shift rightward with it, e.g. shi.bu.há.tan 'place where one has worked'. [p.22] In Thao 'loanwords' the stress is often on the final syllable, realised as length, e.g. /ʃinʃí:/ 'teacher, doctor', /saukhá:/ 'kitchen', /saipú:/ 'preserved radish', /baksá:ŋ/ 'rice dumpling' ... The stress position in Thao is basically the penultimate syllable, but if the suffix is -uan or -iza, the original stem's stress position is retained, while the coda consonant of the stem's final syllable is lengthened to become the onset of -uan or -iza, and stress is then pronounced on the penultimate syllable as well. With the compound suffix -uan-iza the stresses can even reach three.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate, penultimate stress) from Blust 2013. Jian adds the morphological behaviour (prefix/reduplication neutral, suffixes shift stress rightward, -uan/-iza give stem-stress retention plus an extra penult stress), unstressed particles, diphthong handling, and attributes the final-stress class to loanwords realised with length; his /baksá:ŋ/ 'rice dumpling' matches Blust's oxytone example baksán. Blust says some oxytone bases appear native and gives ~2%; Jian frames the final-stress class as loanwords and gives no percentage. Compatible, not contradictory.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole word; prefixation and reduplication leave it on the penult, suffixation shifts it rightward so that it stays penultimate (bú.hat > mu.bú.hat > shi.bu.há.tan). Diphthongs count as two vowels, so stress sits on the penultimate vowel (táun > katáun > kataúnan [ka.táw.nan]). Monosyllables carry the stress; grammatical particles ti, tu, sa, wa, ya are unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such, but Jian describes multiple stresses: with the suffixes -uan and -iza the stem keeps its original (penultimate) stress and an additional stress falls on the penult of the suffixed form (ma.qí.tan.nú.an, lhmi.qá.lhiw.wí.za); with the compound suffix -uan-iza up to three stresses occur (ma.qí.tan.nú.an.ní.za). Derivatives of monosyllabic shnaw show the stress on the prefix or infix syllable (mú.shnaw, mák.shnaw, pák.shnaw, malh.ná.shnaw), i.e. still the penult of the whole word.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Grammatical determiners ti, tu, sa, wa, ya are toneless/unstressed. (2) Loanwords (from Taiwanese/Japanese) typically have final stress realised as vowel length: /ʃinʃí:/ shinshii, /saukhá:/ saukhaa, /saipú:/ saipuu, /baksá:ŋ/ baksaang, /miŋkuiní/ mingkuinii, /pautihí:/ pautihii, /liŋkí:/ lingkii; the orthography writes the long vowel doubled to show both length and stress position. (3) Suffixes -uan, -iza, -uan-iza retain the stem stress and add a penultimate stress (see secondary_stress). (4) Diphthong words: stress on the penultimate vowel, with later glide formation (kataúnan heard as ka.táw.nan).
new_statements.identity_note: Jian 2018 describes Thao as a single language (the Sun Moon Lake community); the stress section names no dialect. Both sources concern the same variety; Blust's 2013 handbook summarises his own 2003 Thao dictionary.
